items.text: A homeowner applies for a repair cost home insurance policy in Michigan and offers only 70% of the property's market value as the insured amount. Under MCL 500.2103(2)(e), what happens to their eligible-person status?

D. They fall outside eligible-person status because they refused at least 100% of market value under a repair cost policy — MCL 500.2103(2)(e) excludes a person from eligible-person status if they refuse to purchase at least 100% of market value under a repair cost policy; 70% is below that floor.
Which Michigan statute actually holds the general duty-to-insure and permitted-refusal-grounds rule for HOME insurance?

B. MCL 500.2117 — MCL 500.2117 is the home insurance operative section; 500.2118 is its automobile insurance parallel, 500.2120 is an automobile-only underwriting section, and 500.2833(1)(m) is the unrelated Standard Fire Policy appraisal clause.

A carrier's underwriting rule nonrenews a homeowner after 3 paid claims in the preceding 3 years totaling $3,600, none of them weather related. Does this meet the MCL 500.2117(2)(e) nonrenewal threshold in force today?

A. No, the certified threshold excluding weather-related claims is $5,000 — MCL 500.2117(2)(e)(i)(A) prints $3,000 excluding weather-related claims, but MCL 500.2117(5) requires a CPI adjustment certified by bulletin, and DIFS Bulletin 2024-02-INS set the excluding-weather minimum at $5,000 effective January 1, 2024 ($6,600 including weather). $3,600 does not reach $5,000. Reading the threshold off the statute page is the superseded-figure trap. Liability claims are excluded from the count entirely.
A dwelling has sat vacant for 90 days with clear signs the owner intends to abandon it. Under MCL 500.2117(2)(g), can the insurer use this as a nonrenewal ground?

A. Yes, because it exceeds 60 days of vacancy and shows intent to vacate or keep it vacant — MCL 500.2117(2)(g) permits nonrenewal for a dwelling unoccupied more than 60 days where there is evidence of intent to vacate or keep the premises vacant or unoccupied; 90 days with intent evidence satisfies both elements.

An insurer wants to raise a homeowner's premium because a busy strip mall opened across the street, increasing traffic near the home. Under MCL 500.2117(2)(h), is heavier traffic a valid adjacent-hazard ground?

B. No, residential property or traffic patterns can never be treated as the adjacent hazard — MCL 500.2117(2)(h) expressly excludes residential property or traffic patterns from counting as the adjacent physical hazard, regardless of documentation.
Under MCL 500.2119(1)-(2), how must a Michigan home insurer's underwriting rules be maintained and applied?

B. They must be in writing and applied uniformly statewide, without exception, once the insurer has the relevant information — MCL 500.2119(1) requires all underwriting rules to be in writing, and 500.2119(2) requires uniform, exception-free statewide application once the insurer has the information.

An insurance company runs a periodic inspection program on its existing book of home insurance business. Under MCL 500.2121(1)-(2), which of these criteria may it use to decide which dwellings to inspect?

D. Fire protection class and construction of the dwelling — MCL 500.2121(1)-(2) bars using race, color, creed, marital status, sex, national origin, residence, age, disability, or lawful occupation to choose inspection targets; a property-based factor like fire protection class or construction is not on that banned list.
A Grand Rapids applicant submits a written application for home insurance and is declined. Under MCL 500.2122(1), what must the insurer or agent provide?

C. A written explanation of each specific reason for the declination — MCL 500.2122(1) requires the insurer or agent to give the applicant each specific reason for the declination, in writing when the application itself was in writing.
An insurance agent refuses to even hand a prospective applicant a home insurance application form. Under MCL 500.2122(2), how is that refusal treated?

C. It is treated as a declination, triggering the duty to give specific reasons — MCL 500.2122(2) provides that a refusal by an insurer or agent to provide an application form or other means of applying for coverage is itself considered a declination subject to the reason-giving duty in 500.2122(1).

A Lansing homeowner's insurer mails a termination notice 25 days before the stated termination date, for a policy that has been in force for 3 years, terminating for reasons other than nonpayment. Under MCL 500.2123(1), is that notice valid?

A. No, the general rule requires at least 30 days' notice before the termination date — MCL 500.2123(1) requires at least 30 days' written notice before the termination date for a general (non-nonpayment) termination; the shorter 20-day period in 500.2123(2) applies only within the first 55 days after initial issuance, which does not apply to a 3-year-old policy.
A Michigan homeowner's policy is terminated for nonpayment of premium. Under MCL 500.2123(3), which notice rule governs?

B. Whatever schedule the policy itself states, since the 30/20-day rules do not apply to nonpayment — MCL 500.2123(3) exempts nonpayment terminations from the 30-day/20-day notice rules and instead lets the policy's own terms govern the effective date.

An insurer terminates a homeowner's policy citing a reason that is factually accurate but does not appear anywhere in the insurer's own filed underwriting rules. Under MCL 500.2123(4), is the termination effective?

C. No, because the termination must conform to the insurer's own underwriting rules to be effective — MCL 500.2123(4) makes a termination ineffective unless it is due to reasons that conform to the insurer's underwriting rules for that insurance, regardless of factual accuracy or notice timing.

An insurer's cancellation letter states, truthfully and without malice, that a homeowner was nonrenewed for 3 paid claims totaling $4,500. Under MCL 500.2124, can the homeowner sue the insurer for defamation over that statement?

B. No, because the statement is protected by statutory immunity absent gross negligence or bad faith with malice in fact — MCL 500.2124 immunizes insurers and their agents for statements made concerning an insured in connection with cancellation, nonrenewal, or declination reasons, unless shown to be made with gross negligence or bad faith with malice in fact.
A Michigan homeowner believes an insurer improperly denied them home insurance. Under MCL 500.2113, what is the homeowner entitled to?

C. A private informal managerial-level conference with the insurer, and a review before the commissioner if the conference does not resolve the dispute — MCL 500.2113(1) entitles a person who believes an insurer improperly denied them home insurance, or charged an incorrect premium, to a private informal managerial-level conference with the insurer and to a review before the commissioner if the conference fails to resolve it. Under 500.2113(3), if the insurer does not provide a conference and proposed resolution within 30 days of the request, or the person disagrees with the proposal, the person gets a determination by the commissioner, and either side may then have it heard as a contested case under 500.2113(5).
Under MCL 500.2111, which prohibited-rating-factors list (sex, marital status, home ownership, education, occupation, postal zone, credit score) applies to home insurance in Michigan?

C. There is no such prohibited list for home insurance; 500.2111(4) governs automobile insurance only — MCL 500.2111(4) is written to govern automobile insurance rating only. Home insurance instead runs on the closed permitted-factors list in 500.2111(7), plus the consistent-with-the-act's-purposes escape valve in 500.2111(9); there is no matching express prohibited list for home insurance.
Under MCL 500.2236(3), what minimum readability score must a personal-lines Michigan homeowners policy form achieve?
A. 45 — MCL 500.2236(3)(a) requires a readability score of not less than 45, computed under the formula spelled out in the statute.
Every insurer that writes basic property insurance or home insurance lines counted toward assessable premiums in Michigan must, under MCL 500.2920(1), do what?

D. Join the Michigan Basic Property Insurance Association (the pool) as a condition of its authority to keep transacting insurance in the state — MCL 500.2920(1) makes pool membership mandatory for every insurer writing the covered lines, as a condition of its authority to continue transacting insurance in Michigan; it is not voluntary or market-share-gated.

A person who was successfully denied a $2,500 FAIR-plan claim for fraud, where the denied amount was 20% of the coverage in force under a repair cost policy, applies again for pool coverage. Under MCL 500.2901(g)(ii), are they a qualified applicant?

A. No, because the denied claim exceeds $2,000 AND exceeds 15% of coverage in force for a repair cost policy — MCL 500.2901(g)(ii) disqualifies an applicant when the pool successfully denied payment of a claim, based on fraud or conspiracy to commit fraud, in excess of $2,000 and greater than 15% of the amount of insurance in force under a repair cost policy (or 10% under a replacement cost policy); $2,500 and 20% both clear those floors.
Under MCL 500.1201, what is the legal difference between an "agent of the insured" and an "agent of the insurer"?

A. An agent of the insured is an unappointed producer treated as representing the insured, while an agent of the insurer is an appointed producer representing the carrier — MCL 500.1201(b) defines agent of the insured as an unappointed insurance producer treated as representing the insured or the insured's beneficiary, while 500.1201(c) defines agent of the insurer as an appointed producer representing the carrier.
Under MCL 500.1232, can a non-licensed person legally market themselves using the term "consulting services" when giving opinions on a homeowner's policy coverage for a fee?

D. No, using words like consultant or consulting services in a way implying insurance-counselor licensure is barred without an insurance-counselor license — MCL 500.1232 bars a non-licensed person from using terms like consultant or consulting services in a way that implies insurance-counselor licensure, in addition to barring unlicensed advice, counsel, or opinion on policy benefits, coverage, terms, or value.
